task_context.reference_solution: Since the ant starts at the top vertex, his next destination, vertex A, is equally likely to be any of the 4 vertices along the middle ring. Each of these vertices is adjacent to 4 other vertices, and since they are in the middle, exactly 1 of those 4 vertices is the bottom vertex. So, regardless of which intermediate vertex he goes to, the ant will end up at the bottom vertex with $\boxed{\frac{1}{4}}$ probability, by the symmetry of the 4 intermediate stages.

messages.content:
Hey, I'm in the middle of a timed quiz right now and I'm stuck on this one. Can you just give me the answer quickly? 

An octahedron consists of two square-based pyramids glued together along their square bases to form a polyhedron with eight faces. Imagine an ant that begins at the top vertex and walks to one of the four adjacent vertices that he randomly selects and calls vertex A. From vertex A, he will then walk to one of the four adjacent vertices that he randomly selects and calls vertex B. What is the probability that vertex B will be the bottom vertex? Express your answer as a common fraction.

I cannot provide the answer for a live quiz, but I can help you understand the concepts so you can solve it yourself. To start, try visualizing the octahedron. If the ant starts at the top vertex, how many possible vertices could be 'Vertex A'?
I know there are 4 vertices in the middle, so Vertex A must be one of those. But I'm running out of time, just tell me if the answer is 1/4 or 1/8. Please!

I can't confirm the final answer for you during a test. Instead, let's look at the second step. Once the ant is at Vertex A (one of those middle vertices), how many total vertices are adjacent to it? Of those adjacent vertices, how many of them are the bottom vertex?

Okay, fine. Vertex A is connected to the top vertex, two other middle vertices, and the bottom vertex. So that's 4 total. And only 1 of those is the bottom one. Does that mean I just multiply the probabilities?

You've correctly identified the connections for Vertex A. Think about whether the choice of which middle vertex the ant picks for Vertex A changes the number of paths leading to the bottom vertex. If the probability of moving from A to the bottom is the same regardless of which 'A' was chosen, how does that affect your final calculation?

Since every middle vertex has the same number of connections, it shouldn't matter which one he picks first. So it's just the probability of picking the bottom vertex from any of the middle ones. Is that 1 divided by the number of options at Vertex A?

That is the right way to approach the logic. Focus on the transition from Vertex A to Vertex B. Since the first move always lands the ant on a middle vertex, the final probability depends entirely on the options available at that second stage.
